Exporting plots and scenes

Source: vignettes/export.Rmd
export.Rmd

Export a panel as a 3D model for another application, or save a projected figure with editable paths and source-row information. This article writes both kinds of output from small plots. Installation is covered in Get started. Optional bridges use rgl, an R package for interactive 3D scenes, and rayrender, an R path tracer.

Example

The built-in motor-car data record weight in thousands of pounds, fuel economy in miles per US gallon and gross horsepower. Model names provide hover text and selection keys. Start with a view of these three variables.

cars <- data.frame(mtcars, model = rownames(mtcars))
p <- ggplot(cars, aes(wt, mpg, z = hp, tooltip = model, data_id = model)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 3, colour = PAL["blue"]) +
  coord_3d() + labs(x = "weight", y = "mpg", z = "horsepower")
p

Model files

export_3d() writes one panel, selected by its index in layout order. The extension chooses the format. The following example writes a binary glTF model, called a GLB file, to a temporary directory and checks the file.

out <- tempfile("ggplot3d-export-")
dir.create(out)
glb <- file.path(out, "cars.glb")
export_3d(p, glb)
file.info(glb)$size > 0
#> [1] TRUE

The glTF 2.0 format transfers meshes, mapped vertex colours, materials and a camera to applications such as Blender. Each layer becomes a named node, so it can be selected and restyled after import. The plot’s vertical axis becomes positive y. An oblique camera is exported as an orthographic camera along its viewing direction.

Keep companion files together when copying an export. Text is omitted from these model formats, and dashed paths become solid. Panes, grid lines and box edges are included with furniture = TRUE.

Extension Contents Companion file
.glb glTF scene and buffer in one binary file None
.gltf glTF scene description .bin buffer
.ply Binary vertices, normals, colours and faces; optional edges None
.obj Objects, vertices, colours and faces .mtl materials
.stl Binary triangles None

Write the other formats with the same call. The temporary directory makes every example runnable without choosing an output folder first.

formats <- c("gltf", "ply", "obj", "stl")
for (extension in formats) {
  export_3d(p, file.path(out, paste0("cars.", extension)))
}
list.files(out)
#> [1] "cars.bin"  "cars.glb"  "cars.gltf" "cars.mtl"  "cars.obj"  "cars.ply" 
#> [7] "cars.stl"

Scale and primitive choices

Model coordinates follow the aspect-scaled panel box. Its longest side is size file units long; expanded scale limits also contribute to that box. PLY and STL use positive z as the vertical axis. OBJ uses positive y. The format’s units are interpreted by the importing application.

Paths become closed tubes with their drawn width as diameter, and markers become small solids. Width and height set the layout used to convert physical line and point sizes relative to the box. Use line and point primitives when the receiving format and software support them.

export_3d(p, file.path(out, "points.ply"), points = "point")
export_3d(p, file.path(out, "large.stl"), size = 50,
  lines = "tube", points = "mesh")
file.info(file.path(out, c("points.ply", "large.stl")))$size > 0
#> [1] TRUE TRUE

STL requires tube paths and mesh points because it stores triangles only. Exporting a surface to STL transfers its triangles; closing the entire model for manufacturing is a separate modelling step. Traced SDF and volume layers produce images in the plot. Use their mesh-producing surface counterparts when exporting model geometry, as shown in Ray marching and volumes.

Animated glTF

animate_3d() writes camera translation, rotation and zoom tracks to glTF. The first panel is exported. Start with a three-frame turn of the same motor cars; the result records the file and frame count.

turn <- animate_3d(p, azimuth = c(-60, -20, 20), frames = 3,
  file = file.path(out, "turn.glb"), fps = 2, width = 320, height = 320,
  workers = 1, progress = FALSE)
turn$frame_count
#> [1] 3

For changing data, a time column selects the rows drawn in each frame. Scales train on all frames, and visibility tracks select the frame’s geometry in the file. Here the horsepower coordinate increases by twenty in the second frame. These changed coordinates are an illustration of animation.

states <- rbind(transform(cars, step = 1),
  transform(cars, step = 2, hp = hp + 20))
changing <- ggplot(states, aes(wt, mpg, z = hp)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 3, colour = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
motion <- animate_3d(changing, time = "step", azimuth = -60,
  file = file.path(out, "states.gltf"), fps = 2,
  width = 320, height = 320, workers = 1, progress = FALSE)
motion$frame_count
#> [1] 2

Keep a projection type fixed within an animation. Camera paths and frame timing are described in Camera animation and interaction.

rgl meshes and scenes

The rgl bridge dispatches through its own generic functions. Convert the plot to a mesh with vertex colours, then inspect the vertex and triangle counts. Point primitives can instead populate the mesh’s point indices.

mesh <- rgl::as.mesh3d(p)
c(vertices = ncol(mesh$vb), triangles = ncol(mesh$it))
#>  vertices triangles 
#>      7680      2560

Draw with the plot’s camera angles and projection through rgl::plot3d(). This example uses rgl’s null device so it also runs during document builds. rgl centres the drawn geometry itself, so its framing may differ from the original plot. The scene includes text through rgl’s native text primitives.

old <- options(rgl.useNULL = TRUE)
ids <- rgl::plot3d(p)
length(ids)
#> [1] 1
rgl::close3d()
options(old)

rayrender scenes

Build a rayrender scene to continue with that package’s materials, lights and renderer. The bridge creates one diffuse mesh object per nonempty geometry layer, with the mapped vertex colours. Paths become tubes and points become solids; translucency is omitted.

scene <- as_rayrender_3d(p)
nrow(scene)
#> [1] 1

Setting render = TRUE passes the scene and plot camera to rayrender’s renderer. Additional arguments control that render. The native path tracer in Ray marching and volumes provides diffuse rendering directly within a ggplot panel.

Semantic SVG

The native Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) writer preserves the connection between a visible fragment and its source layer and row. Hovering or focusing a fragment highlights fragments from the same source row, and its title provides tooltip text. The projected view stays fixed.

svg <- file.path(out, "cars.svg")
save_svg_3d(p, svg, interactive = TRUE, width = 624, height = 432)
doc <- xml2::read_xml(svg)
fragments <- xml2::xml_find_all(doc, ".//*[@data-primitive]")
head(unique(xml2::xml_attr(fragments, "data-layer")))
#> [1] "0" "1"

Each fragment carries data-layer, data-row and data-primitive attributes. Consecutive runs from each layer are grouped in paint order, preserving depth ordering across layers. Clipping paths and compound seam underlays retain the visibility of the compiled vector scene. Set interactive = FALSE for a file without the hover script.

The embedded preview below retains hover and keyboard interaction. It uses an HTML object containing the exported SVG itself.

Open the SVG directly in a browser or embed it as an HTML object to retain its interaction. An SVG displayed through an image element supplies a static preview. Interactive viewing provides a camera you can rotate.

TikZ

TikZ is a LaTeX drawing language. Export the whole projected plot as editable fill, draw, text and clipping commands. The standalone setting includes a document preamble; disable it for code to insert into an existing document.

tikz <- export_code_3d(p, "tikz", file = file.path(out, "cars.tex"))
cat(paste(head(strsplit(tikz, "\n")[[1]], 5), collapse = "\n"))
#> \documentclass[tikz,border=0pt]{standalone}
#> \usepackage{graphicx}
#> \usetikzlibrary{svg.path}
#> \begin{document}
#> \begin{tikzpicture}[x=1pt,y=1pt]

Compile the file with pdflatex cars.tex. The generated code uses TikZ’s svg.path library, and TeX selects the text font. Raster colourbars and annotations become coloured pixel rectangles. The complete figure includes all panels, furniture and legends.

Asymptote and PRC

Asymptote is a language for mathematical graphics. Its exporter writes model-space geometry, materials, text and a camera, which you can edit to render another view. The panel index selects the scene to export.

asy <- export_code_3d(p, "asy", panel = 1,
  file = file.path(out, "cars.asy"), prc = TRUE)
cat(paste(head(strsplit(asy, "\n")[[1]], 5), collapse = "\n"))
#> settings.prc=true;
#> import three;
#> size(169.333333333mm,169.333333333mm);
#> currentprojection=orthographic(camera=(1.68301270189,-1.54903810568,1.86602540378),up=(-0.250000000000,0.433012701892,0.866025403784),target=(0.500000000000,0.500000000000,0.500000000000),center=false);
#> surface ggplotModel;

The PRC setting requests embedded 3D content in PDF. Compile with asy -tex pdflatex -f pdf cars.asy and install the TeX packages media9 and ocgx2. A PDF reader with PRC support supplies the interactive view. For a static PDF or ordinary SVG through an R graphics device, use Output backends. ## 3D printing

print_3d() maps the panel box into a physical bounding box in millimetres, keeping its aspect. Tube widths, marker sizes, shell thicknesses and the base plate are applied in millimetres after scaling. Open surfaces can become normal-offset shells or close vertically onto the base. Layer overrides use the exported layer names, such as c(layer1_surface = "base").

settings <- print_3d(size_mm = c(100, 100, 60), min_mm = 0.8,
  shell_mm = 1.2, base_mm = 2, text = "raised", furniture = c("base", "axes"))
export_3d(p, "cars.stl", print = settings)
export_3d(p, "cars.3mf", print = settings)

Printing uses the bundled Manifold C++ library for Boolean union with double-precision meshes and colour propagation. Native checks validate edge incidence, closure, winding and self-intersection and identify failing layers. Disconnected closed components share one exported model object.

Character labels use font outlines extruded on backing plaques. Raised labels project from the plaque; engraved labels cut into it. text = "none" omits labels. Axis geometry follows the plot’s in-plane guide layout. Furniture and text can extend beyond the panel bounding box, so check the full model bounds in the slicer before printing.

Binary STL stores geometry. 3MF stores millimetre units and triangle colours using the 3MF Materials and Properties colour-group extension. Import and re-export checks with PrusaSlicer 2.9.7 and Bambu Studio 2.9.1.70 preserved the test model’s geometry and omitted its standard colour groups. Assigning these colours to printer filaments requires support in the target slicer; vendor paint formats are separate extensions.
